summary: This RFC defines a Telnet option for marking the end of a record in data sent over a Telnet connection. It is a proposed standard. Some applications need clear record boundaries in what would otherwise be a plain stream of characters.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet sends data as a plain stream of characters, which makes it hard to see where one record ends and the next begins. This option lets the two ends agree on a marker that says a record has ended, and each direction is agreed on separately.

questions: how to mark end of record in telnet
what is the telnet end of record option
what is iac eor in telnet
how is the end of record option negotiated
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets each side mark where a record of data ends.

tldr.problem: Some systems end a unit of data with a special key rather than an ordinary character, and plain Telnet has no standard way to say where such a unit ends.
tldr.mechanism: The END-OF-RECORD option, code 25, is negotiated with WILL, WON'T, DO and DON'T, after which the sender marks the end of each record with the two-octet sequence IAC EOR.
tldr.outcome: Both ends can agree on record boundaries inside a Telnet stream, negotiated separately for each direction. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 885 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Mark the End of a Record
sections.content:
Many interactive systems use one of the normal data characters, for example carriage-return, line-feed or escape, to indicate the end of an effective unit of data, called a record. Some systems instead have a special means of indicating the end of a data unit, such as a special key. This Telnet option provides a standard way to communicate the end of a data unit.

The option is named END-OF-RECORD and has code 25.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers mark the end of a chunk of data with a normal character; others use a special key. This option gives every system one common way to mark that boundary.

sections.title: Negotiating the Option
sections.content:
The usual Telnet option commands apply. IAC WILL END-OF-RECORD asks permission to begin transmitting EOR codes, or confirms that the sender will now begin sending them. IAC DO END-OF-RECORD requests that the sender of data start transmitting EORs, or confirms that it is expected to. IAC WON'T and IAC DON'T refuse or demand a stop.

The default is WON'T END-OF-RECORD and DON'T END-OF-RECORD, so no EOR is transmitted. The two parties will probably transmit EORs in both directions if they use them at all, but their use must be negotiated independently for each direction.
sections.plainLanguage: One side asks to use the marker, and the other agrees or refuses. Each direction of the conversation is agreed on its own, and the option is off by default.

sections.title: How the Option Behaves
sections.content:
When the END-OF-RECORD option is in effect between a sender and a receiver of the data, the sender transmits EORs. The end of a record is indicated by the IAC EOR two-octet sequence, and the code for EOR is 239 (decimal).

When the option is not in effect, a received IAC EOR should be treated as a NOP, although it should not normally be sent in that mode. Because EOR marks the end of an effective data unit, Telnet should try to send the data up to and including the EOR code together, to promote communication efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: The marker is the two-octet sequence IAC EOR. If the option is off, a stray marker is simply ignored. Telnet tries to send each record and its marker in one piece.

items.label: WILL
items.desc: Sender asks to begin, or confirms it will begin, transmitting EORs.

items.label: WON'T
items.desc: Sender demands to stop, or refuses to begin, transmitting EORs.

items.label: DO
items.desc: Sender asks the data sender to start transmitting EORs, or confirms it is expected to.

items.label: DON'T
items.desc: Sender demands the receiver stop or not start transmitting EORs.
